90: ## Pod phase
91: 
92: A Pod's `status` field is a
93: [PodStatus](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#podstatus-v1-core)
94: object, which has a `phase` field.
95: 
96: The phase of a Pod is a simple, high-level summary of where the Pod is in its
97: lifecycle. The phase is not intended to be a comprehensive rollup of observations
98: of container or Pod state, nor is it intended to be a comprehensive state machine.
99: 
100: The number and meanings of Pod phase values are tightly guarded.
101: Other than what is documented here, nothing should be assumed about Pods that
102: have a given `phase` value.
103: 
104: Here are the possible values for `phase`:
105: 
106: Value       | Description
107: :-----------|:-----------
108: `Pending`   | The Pod has been accepted by the Kubernetes cluster, but one or more of the containers has not been set up and made ready to run. This includes time a Pod spends waiting to be scheduled as well as the time spent downloading container images over the network.
109: `Running`   | The Pod has been bound to a node, and all of the containers have been created. At least one container is still running, or is in the process of starting or restarting.
110: `Succeeded` | All containers in the Pod have terminated in success, and will not be restarted.
111: `Failed`    | All containers in the Pod have terminated, and at least one container has terminated in failure. That is, the container either exited with non-zero status or was terminated by the system, and is not set for automatic restarting.
112: `Unknown`   | For some reason the state of the Pod could not be obtained. This phase typically occurs due to an error in communicating with the node where the Pod should be running.
113: 
114: {{< note >}}
115: 
116: When a pod is failing to start repeatedly, `CrashLoopBackOff` may appear in the `Status` field of some kubectl commands. Similarly, when a pod is being deleted, `Terminating` may appear in the `Status` field of some kubectl commands. 
117: 
118: Make sure not to confuse _Status_, a kubectl display field for user intuition, with the pod's `phase`.
119: Pod phase is an explicit part of the Kubernetes data model and of the
120: [Pod API](/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1/). 
121: 
122: ```
123:   NAMESPACE               NAME               READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
124:   alessandras-namespace   alessandras-pod    0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   200        2d9h
125: ```
126: 
127: ---
128: 
129: A Pod is granted a term to terminate gracefully, which defaults to 30 seconds.
130: You can use the flag `--force` to [terminate a Pod by force](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination-forced).
131: {{< /note >}}
132: 
133: Since Kubernetes 1.27, the kubelet transitions deleted Pods, except for
134: [static Pods](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/static-pod/) and
135: [force-deleted Pods](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination-forced)
136: without a finalizer, to a terminal phase (`Failed` or `Succeeded` depending on
137: the exit statuses of the pod containers) before their deletion from the API server.
138: 
139: If a node dies or is disconnected from the rest of the cluster, Kubernetes
140: applies a policy for setting the `phase` of all Pods on the lost node to Failed.
141: 
142: ## Container states
143: 
144: As well as the [phase](#pod-phase) of the Pod overall, Kubernetes tracks the state of
145: each container inside a Pod. You can use
146: [container lifecycle hooks](/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks/) to
147: trigger events to run at certain points in a container's lifecycle.
148: 
149: Once the {{< glossary_tooltip text="scheduler" term_id="kube-scheduler" >}}
150: assigns a Pod to a Node, the kubelet starts creating containers for that Pod
151: using a {{< glossary_tooltip text="container runtime" term_id="container-runtime" >}}.
152: There are three possible container states: `Waiting`, `Running`, and `Terminated`.
153: 
154: To check the state of a Pod's containers, you can use
155: `kubectl describe pod <name-of-pod>`. The output shows the state for each container
156: within that Pod.
157: 
158: Each state has a specific meaning:
159: 
160: ### `Waiting` {#container-state-waiting}
161: 
162: If a container is not in either the `Running` or `Terminated` state, it is `Waiting`.
163: A container in the `Waiting` state is still running the operations it requires in
164: order to complete start up: for example, pulling the container image from a container
165: image registry, or applying {{< glossary_tooltip text="Secret" term_id="secret" >}}
166: data.
167: When you use `kubectl` to query a Pod with a container that is `Waiting`, you also see
168: a Reason field to summarize why the container is in that state.
169: 
170: ### `Running` {#container-state-running}
171: 
172: The `Running` status indicates that a container is executing without issues. If there
173: was a `postStart` hook configured, it has already executed and finished. When you use
174: `kubectl` to query a Pod with a container that is `Running`, you also see information
175: about when the container entered the `Running` state.
176: 
177: ### `Terminated` {#container-state-terminated}
178: 
179: A container in the `Terminated` state began execution and then either ran to
180: completion or failed for some reason. When you use `kubectl` to query a Pod with
181: a container that is `Terminated`, you see a reason, an exit code, and the start and
182: finish time for that container's period of execution.
183: 
184: If a container has a `preStop` hook configured, this hook runs before the container enters
185: the `Terminated` state.
186: 
187: ## How Pods handle problems with containers {#container-restarts}
188: 
189: Kubernetes manages container failures within Pods using a [`restartPolicy`](#restart-policy) defined in the Pod `spec`. This policy determines how Kubernetes reacts to containers exiting due to errors or other reasons, which falls in the following sequence:
190: 
191: 1. **Initial crash**: Kubernetes attempts an immediate restart based on the Pod `restartPolicy`.
192: 1. **Repeated crashes**: After the initial crash Kubernetes applies an exponential
193:    backoff delay for subsequent restarts, described in [`restartPolicy`](#restart-policy).
194:    This prevents rapid, repeated restart attempts from overloading the system.
195: 1. **CrashLoopBackOff state**: This indicates that the backoff delay mechanism is currently
196:    in effect for a given container that is in a crash loop, failing and restarting repeatedly.
197: 1. **Backoff reset**: If a container runs successfully for a certain duration
198:    (e.g., 10 minutes), Kubernetes resets the backoff delay, treating any new crash
199:    as the first one.
200: 
201: In practice, a `CrashLoopBackOff` is a condition or event that might be seen as output
202: from the `kubectl` command, while describing or listing Pods, when a container in the Pod
203: fails to start properly and then continually tries and fails in a loop.
204: 
205: In other words, when a container enters the crash loop, Kubernetes applies the
206: exponential backoff delay mentioned in the [Container restart policy](#restart-policy).
207: This mechanism prevents a faulty container from overwhelming the system with continuous
208: failed start attempts.
209: 
210: The `CrashLoopBackOff` can be caused by issues like the following:
211: 
212: * Application errors that cause the container to exit.
213: * Configuration errors, such as incorrect environment variables or missing
214:   configuration files.
215: * Resource constraints, where the container might not have enough memory or CPU
216:   to start properly.
217: * Health checks failing if the application doesn't start serving within the
218:   expected time.
219: * Container liveness probes or startup probes returning a `Failure` result
220:   as mentioned in the [probes section](#container-probes).
221: 
222: To investigate the root cause of a `CrashLoopBackOff` issue, a user can:
223: 
224: 1. **Check logs**: Use `kubectl logs <name-of-pod>` to check the logs of the container.
225:    This is often the most direct way to diagnose the issue causing the crashes.
226: 1. **Inspect events**: Use `kubectl describe pod <name-of-pod>` to see events
227:    for the Pod, which can provide hints about configuration or resource issues.
228: 1. **Review configuration**: Ensure that the Pod configuration, including
229:    environment variables and mounted volumes, is correct and that all required
230:    external resources are available.
231: 1. **Check resource limits**: Make sure that the container has enough CPU
232:    and memory allocated. Sometimes, increasing the resources in the Pod definition
233:    can resolve the issue.
234: 1. **Debug application**: There might exist bugs or misconfigurations in the
235:    application code. Running this container image locally or in a development
236:    environment can help diagnose application specific issues.

238: ### Container restart policy {#restart-policy}
239: 
240: The `spec` of a Pod has a `restartPolicy` field with possible values Always, OnFailure,
241: and Never. The default value is Always.
242: 
243: The `restartPolicy` for a Pod applies to {{< glossary_tooltip text="app containers" term_id="app-container" >}}
244: in the Pod and to regular [init containers](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/init-containers/).
245: [Sidecar containers](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/sidecar-containers/)
246: ignore the Pod-level `restartPolicy` field: in Kubernetes, a sidecar is defined as an
247: entry inside `initContainers` that has its container-level `restartPolicy` set to `Always`.
248: For init containers that exit with an error, the kubelet restarts the init container if
249: the Pod level `restartPolicy` is either `OnFailure` or `Always`:
250: 
251: * `Always`: Automatically restarts the container after any termination.
252: * `OnFailure`: Only restarts the container if it exits with an error (non-zero exit status).
253: * `Never`: Does not automatically restart the terminated container.
254: 
255: When the kubelet is handling container restarts according to the configured restart
256: policy, that only applies to restarts that make replacement containers inside the
257: same Pod and running on the same node. After containers in a Pod exit, the kubelet
258: restarts them with an exponential backoff delay (10s, 20s, 40s, …), that is capped at
259: 300 seconds (5 minutes). Once a container has executed for 10 minutes without any
260: problems, the kubelet resets the restart backoff timer for that container.
261: [Sidecar containers and Pod lifecycle](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/sidecar-containers/#sidecar-containers-and-pod-lifecycle)
262: explains the behaviour of `init containers` when specify `restartpolicy` field on it.
263: 
264: ### Configurable container restart delay
265: 
266: {{< feature-state feature_gate_name="KubeletCrashLoopBackOffMax" >}}
267: 
268: With the alpha feature gate `KubeletCrashLoopBackOffMax` enabled, you can
269: reconfigure the maximum delay between container start retries from the default
270: of 300s (5 minutes). This configuration is set per node using kubelet
271: configuration. In your [kubelet configuration](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-config-file/),
272: under `crashLoopBackOff` set the `maxContainerRestartPeriod` field between
273: `"1s"` and `"300s"`. As described above in [Container restart
274: policy](#restart-policy), delays on that node will still start at 10s and
275: increase exponentially by 2x each restart, but will now be capped at your
276: configured maximum. If the `maxContainerRestartPeriod` you configure is less
277: than the default initial value of 10s, the initial delay will instead be set to
278: the configured maximum.
279: 
280: See the following kubelet configuration examples:
281: 
282: ```yaml
283: # container restart delays will start at 10s, increasing
284: # 2x each time they are restarted, to a maximum of 100s
285: kind: KubeletConfiguration
286: crashLoopBackOff:
287:     maxContainerRestartPeriod: "100s"
288: ```
289: 
290: ```yaml
291: # delays between container restarts will always be 2s
292: kind: KubeletConfiguration
293: crashLoopBackOff:
294:     maxContainerRestartPeriod: "2s"
295: ```

297: ## Pod conditions
298: 
299: A Pod has a PodStatus, which has an array of
300: [PodConditions](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#podcondition-v1-core)
301: through which the Pod has or has not passed. Kubelet manages the following
302: PodConditions:
303: 
304: * `PodScheduled`: the Pod has been scheduled to a node.
305: * `PodReadyToStartContainers`: (beta feature; enabled by [default](#pod-has-network)) the
306:   Pod sandbox has been successfully created and networking configured.
307: * `ContainersReady`: all containers in the Pod are ready.
308: * `Initialized`: all [init containers](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/init-containers/)
309:   have completed successfully.
310: * `Ready`: the Pod is able to serve requests and should be added to the load
311:   balancing pools of all matching Services.
312: 
313: Field name           | Description
314: :--------------------|:-----------
315: `type`               | Name of this Pod condition.
316: `status`             | Indicates whether that condition is applicable, with possible values "`True`", "`False`", or "`Unknown`".
317: `lastProbeTime`      | Timestamp of when the Pod condition was last probed.
318: `lastTransitionTime` | Timestamp for when the Pod last transitioned from one status to another.
319: `reason`             | Machine-readable, UpperCamelCase text indicating the reason for the condition's last transition.
320: `message`            | Human-readable message indicating details about the last status transition.
321: 
322: 
323: ### Pod readiness {#pod-readiness-gate}
324: 
325: {{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.14" state="stable" >}}
326: 
327: Your application can inject extra feedback or signals into PodStatus:
328: _Pod readiness_. To use this, set `readinessGates` in the Pod's `spec` to
329: specify a list of additional conditions that the kubelet evaluates for Pod readiness.
330: 
331: Readiness gates are determined by the current state of `status.condition`
332: fields for the Pod. If Kubernetes cannot find such a condition in the
333: `status.conditions` field of a Pod, the status of the condition
334: is defaulted to "`False`".
335: 
336: Here is an example:
337: 
338: ```yaml
339: kind: Pod
340: ...
341: spec:
342:   readinessGates:
343:     - conditionType: "www.example.com/feature-1"
344: status:
345:   conditions:
346:     - type: Ready                              # a built in PodCondition
347:       status: "False"
348:       lastProbeTime: null
349:       lastTransitionTime: 2018-01-01T00:00:00Z
350:     - type: "www.example.com/feature-1"        # an extra PodCondition
351:       status: "False"
352:       lastProbeTime: null
353:       lastTransitionTime: 2018-01-01T00:00:00Z
354:   containerStatuses:
355:     - containerID: docker://abcd...
356:       ready: true
357: ...
358: ```
359: 
360: The Pod conditions you add must have names that meet the Kubernetes
361: [label key format](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#syntax-and-character-set).
362: 
363: ### Status for Pod readiness {#pod-readiness-status}
364: 
365: The `kubectl patch` command does not support patching object status.
366: To set these `status.conditions` for the Pod, applications and
367: {{< glossary_tooltip term_id="operator-pattern" text="operators">}} should use
368: the `PATCH` action.
369: You can use a [Kubernetes client library](/docs/reference/using-api/client-libraries/) to
370: write code that sets custom Pod conditions for Pod readiness.
371: 
372: For a Pod that uses custom conditions, that Pod is evaluated to be ready **only**
373: when both the following statements apply:
374: 
375: * All containers in the Pod are ready.
376: * All conditions specified in `readinessGates` are `True`.
377: 
378: When a Pod's containers are Ready but at least one custom condition is missing or
379: `False`, the kubelet sets the Pod's [condition](#pod-conditions) to `ContainersReady`.
380: 
381: ### Pod network readiness {#pod-has-network}
382: 
383: {{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.29" state="beta" >}}
384: 
385: {{< note >}}
386: During its early development, this condition was named `PodHasNetwork`.
387: {{< /note >}}
388: 
389: After a Pod gets scheduled on a node, it needs to be admitted by the kubelet and
390: to have any required storage volumes mounted. Once these phases are complete,
391: the kubelet works with
392: a container runtime (using {{< glossary_tooltip term_id="cri" >}}) to set up a
393: runtime sandbox and configure networking for the Pod. If the
394: `PodReadyToStartContainersCondition`
395: [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/) is enabled
396: (it is enabled by default for Kubernetes {{< skew currentVersion >}}), the
397: `PodReadyToStartContainers` condition will be added to the `status.conditions` field of a Pod.
398: 
399: The `PodReadyToStartContainers` condition is set to `False` by the Kubelet when it detects a
400: Pod does not have a runtime sandbox with networking configured. This occurs in
401: the following scenarios:
402: 
403: - Early in the lifecycle of the Pod, when the kubelet has not yet begun to set up a sandbox for
404:   the Pod using the container runtime.
405: - Later in the lifecycle of the Pod, when the Pod sandbox has been destroyed due to either:
406:   - the node rebooting, without the Pod getting evicted
407:   - for container runtimes that use virtual machines for isolation, the Pod
408:     sandbox virtual machine rebooting, which then requires creating a new sandbox and
409:     fresh container network configuration.
410: 
411: The `PodReadyToStartContainers` condition is set to `True` by the kubelet after the
412: successful completion of sandbox creation and network configuration for the Pod
413: by the runtime plugin. The kubelet can start pulling container images and create
414: containers after `PodReadyToStartContainers` condition has been set to `True`.
415: 
416: For a Pod with init containers, the kubelet sets the `Initialized` condition to
417: `True` after the init containers have successfully completed (which happens
418: after successful sandbox creation and network configuration by the runtime
419: plugin). For a Pod without init containers, the kubelet sets the `Initialized`
420: condition to `True` before sandbox creation and network configuration starts.

422: ## Container probes
423: 
424: A _probe_ is a diagnostic performed periodically by the [kubelet](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/)
425: on a container. To perform a diagnostic, the kubelet either executes code within the container,
426: or makes a network request.
427: 
428: ### Check mechanisms {#probe-check-methods}
429: 
430: There are four different ways to check a container using a probe.
431: Each probe must define exactly one of these four mechanisms:
432: 
433: `exec`
434: : Executes a specified command inside the container. The diagnostic
435:   is considered successful if the command exits with a status code of 0.
436: 
437: `grpc`
438: : Performs a remote procedure call using [gRPC](https://grpc.io/).
439:   The target should implement
440:   [gRPC health checks](https://grpc.io/grpc/core/md_doc_health-checking.html).
441:   The diagnostic is considered successful if the `status`
442:   of the response is `SERVING`.  
443: 
444: `httpGet`
445: : Performs an HTTP `GET` request against the Pod's IP
446:   address on a specified port and path. The diagnostic is
447:   considered successful if the response has a status code
448:   greater than or equal to 200 and less than 400.
449: 
450: `tcpSocket`
451: : Performs a TCP check against the Pod's IP address on
452:   a specified port. The diagnostic is considered successful if
453:   the port is open. If the remote system (the container) closes
454:   the connection immediately after it opens, this counts as healthy.
455: 
456: {{< caution >}} Unlike the other mechanisms, `exec` probe's implementation involves the creation/forking of multiple processes each time when executed.
457: As a result, in case of the clusters having higher pod densities, lower intervals of `initialDelaySeconds`, `periodSeconds`, configuring any probe with exec mechanism might introduce an overhead on the cpu usage of the node.
458: In such scenarios, consider using the alternative probe mechanisms to avoid the overhead.{{< /caution >}}
459: 
460: ### Probe outcome
461: 
462: Each probe has one of three results:
463: 
464: `Success`
465: : The container passed the diagnostic.
466: 
467: `Failure`
468: : The container failed the diagnostic.
469: 
470: `Unknown`
471: : The diagnostic failed (no action should be taken, and the kubelet
472:   will make further checks).
473: 
474: ### Types of probe
475: 
476: The kubelet can optionally perform and react to three kinds of probes on running
477: containers:
478: 
479: `livenessProbe`
480: : Indicates whether the container is running. If
481:   the liveness probe fails, the kubelet kills the container, and the container
482:   is subjected to its [restart policy](#restart-policy). If a container does not
483:   provide a liveness probe, the default state is `Success`.
484: 
485: `readinessProbe`
486: : Indicates whether the container is ready to respond to requests.
487:   If the readiness probe fails, the endpoints controller removes the Pod's IP
488:   address from the endpoints of all Services that match the Pod. The default
489:   state of readiness before the initial delay is `Failure`. If a container does
490:   not provide a readiness probe, the default state is `Success`.
491: 
492: `startupProbe`
493: : Indicates whether the application within the container is started.
494:   All other probes are disabled if a startup probe is provided, until it succeeds.
495:   If the startup probe fails, the kubelet kills the container, and the container
496:  is subjected to its [restart policy](#restart-policy). If a container does not
497:   provide a startup probe, the default state is `Success`.
498: 
499: For more information about how to set up a liveness, readiness, or startup probe,
500: see [Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/).
501: 
502: #### When should you use a liveness probe?
503: 
504: If the process in your container is able to crash on its own whenever it
505: encounters an issue or becomes unhealthy, you do not necessarily need a liveness
506: probe; the kubelet will automatically perform the correct action in accordance
507: with the Pod's `restartPolicy`.
508: 
509: If you'd like your container to be killed and restarted if a probe fails, then
510: specify a liveness probe, and specify a `restartPolicy` of Always or OnFailure.
511: 
512: #### When should you use a readiness probe?
513: 
514: If you'd like to start sending traffic to a Pod only when a probe succeeds,
515: specify a readiness probe. In this case, the readiness probe might be the same
516: as the liveness probe, but the existence of the readiness probe in the spec means
517: that the Pod will start without receiving any traffic and only start receiving
518: traffic after the probe starts succeeding.
519: 
520: If you want your container to be able to take itself down for maintenance, you
521: can specify a readiness probe that checks an endpoint specific to readiness that
522: is different from the liveness probe.
523: 
524: If your app has a strict dependency on back-end services, you can implement both
525: a liveness and a readiness probe. The liveness probe passes when the app itself
526: is healthy, but the readiness probe additionally checks that each required
527: back-end service is available. This helps you avoid directing traffic to Pods
528: that can only respond with error messages.
529: 
530: If your container needs to work on loading large data, configuration files, or
531: migrations during startup, you can use a
532: [startup probe](#when-should-you-use-a-startup-probe). However, if you want to
533: detect the difference between an app that has failed and an app that is still
534: processing its startup data, you might prefer a readiness probe.
535: 
536: {{< note >}}
537: If you want to be able to drain requests when the Pod is deleted, you do not
538: necessarily need a readiness probe; on deletion, the Pod automatically puts itself
539: into an unready state regardless of whether the readiness probe exists.
540: The Pod remains in the unready state while it waits for the containers in the Pod
541: to stop.
542: {{< /note >}}
543: 
544: #### When should you use a startup probe?
545: 
546: Startup probes are useful for Pods that have containers that take a long time to
547: come into service. Rather than set a long liveness interval, you can configure
548: a separate configuration for probing the container as it starts up, allowing
549: a time longer than the liveness interval would allow.
550: 
551: <!-- ensure front matter contains math: true -->
552: If your container usually starts in more than
553: \\( initialDelaySeconds + failureThreshold \times  periodSeconds \\), you should specify a
554: startup probe that checks the same endpoint as the liveness probe. The default for
555: `periodSeconds` is 10s. You should then set its `failureThreshold` high enough to
556: allow the container to start, without changing the default values of the liveness
557: probe. This helps to protect against deadlocks.

559: ## Termination of Pods {#pod-termination}
560: 
561: Because Pods represent processes running on nodes in the cluster, it is important to
562: allow those processes to gracefully terminate when they are no longer needed (rather
563: than being abruptly stopped with a `KILL` signal and having no chance to clean up).
564: 
565: The design aim is for you to be able to request deletion and know when processes
566: terminate, but also be able to ensure that deletes eventually complete.
567: When you request deletion of a Pod, the cluster records and tracks the intended grace period
568: before the Pod is allowed to be forcefully killed. With that forceful shutdown tracking in
569: place, the {{< glossary_tooltip text="kubelet" term_id="kubelet" >}} attempts graceful
570: shutdown.
571: 
572: Typically, with this graceful termination of the pod, kubelet makes requests to the container runtime to attempt to stop the containers in the pod by first sending a TERM (aka. SIGTERM) signal, with a grace period timeout, to the main process in each container. The requests to stop the containers are processed by the container runtime asynchronously. There is no guarantee to the order of processing for these requests. Many container runtimes respect the `STOPSIGNAL` value defined in the container image and, if different, send the container image configured STOPSIGNAL instead of TERM.
573: Once the grace period has expired, the KILL signal is sent to any remaining
574: processes, and the Pod is then deleted from the
575: {{< glossary_tooltip text="API Server" term_id="kube-apiserver" >}}. If the kubelet or the
576: container runtime's management service is restarted while waiting for processes to terminate, the
577: cluster retries from the start including the full original grace period.
578: 
579: Pod termination flow, illustrated with an example:
580: 
581: 1. You use the `kubectl` tool to manually delete a specific Pod, with the default grace period
582:    (30 seconds).
583: 
584: 1. The Pod in the API server is updated with the time beyond which the Pod is considered "dead"
585:    along with the grace period.
586:    If you use `kubectl describe` to check the Pod you're deleting, that Pod shows up as "Terminating".
587:    On the node where the Pod is running: as soon as the kubelet sees that a Pod has been marked
588:    as terminating (a graceful shutdown duration has been set), the kubelet begins the local Pod
589:    shutdown process.
590: 
591:    1. If one of the Pod's containers has defined a `preStop`
592:       [hook](/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks) and the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`
593:       in the Pod spec is not set to 0, the kubelet runs that hook inside of the container.
594:       The default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is 30 seconds.
595: 
596:       If the `preStop` hook is still running after the grace period expires, the kubelet requests
597:       a small, one-off grace period extension of 2 seconds.
598:    {{% note %}}
599:    If the `preStop` hook needs longer to complete than the default grace period allows,
600:    you must modify `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to suit this.
601:    {{% /note %}}
602: 
603:    1. The kubelet triggers the container runtime to send a TERM signal to process 1 inside each
604:       container.
605: 
606:       There is [special ordering](#termination-with-sidecars) if the Pod has any
607:       {{< glossary_tooltip text="sidecar containers" term_id="sidecar-container" >}} defined.
608:       Otherwise, the containers in the Pod receive the TERM signal at different times and in
609:       an arbitrary order. If the order of shutdowns matters, consider using a `preStop` hook
610:       to synchronize (or switch to using sidecar containers).
611: 
612: 1. At the same time as the kubelet is starting graceful shutdown of the Pod, the control plane
613:    evaluates whether to remove that shutting-down Pod from EndpointSlice (and Endpoints) objects,
614:    where those objects represent a {{< glossary_tooltip term_id="service" text="Service" >}}
615:    with a configured {{< glossary_tooltip text="selector" term_id="selector" >}}.
616:    {{< glossary_tooltip text="ReplicaSets" term_id="replica-set" >}} and other workload resources
617:    no longer treat the shutting-down Pod as a valid, in-service replica.
618: 
619:    Pods that shut down slowly should not continue to serve regular traffic and should start
620:    terminating and finish processing open connections.  Some applications need to go beyond
621:    finishing open connections and need more graceful termination, for example, session draining
622:    and completion.
623: 
624:    Any endpoints that represent the terminating Pods are not immediately removed from
625:    EndpointSlices, and a status indicating [terminating state](/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices/#conditions)
626:    is exposed from the EndpointSlice API (and the legacy Endpoints API).
627:    Terminating endpoints always have their `ready` status as `false` (for backward compatibility
628:    with versions before 1.26), so load balancers will not use it for regular traffic.
629: 
630:    If traffic draining on terminating Pod is needed, the actual readiness can be checked as a
631:    condition `serving`.  You can find more details on how to implement connections draining in the
632:    tutorial [Pods And Endpoints Termination Flow](/docs/tutorials/services/pods-and-endpoint-termination-flow/)
633: 
634:    <a id="pod-termination-beyond-grace-period" />
635: 
636: 1. The kubelet ensures the Pod is shut down and terminated
637:    1. When the grace period expires, if there is still any container running in the Pod, the
638:       kubelet triggers forcible shutdown.
639:       The container runtime sends `SIGKILL` to any processes still running in any container in the Pod.
640:       The kubelet also cleans up a hidden `pause` container if that container runtime uses one.
641:    1. The kubelet transitions the Pod into a terminal phase (`Failed` or `Succeeded` depending on
642:       the end state of its containers).
643:    1. The kubelet triggers forcible removal of the Pod object from the API server, by setting grace period
644:       to 0 (immediate deletion).
645:    1. The API server deletes the Pod's API object, which is then no longer visible from any client.
646: 
647: 
648: ### Forced Pod termination {#pod-termination-forced}
649: 
650: {{< caution >}}
651: Forced deletions can be potentially disruptive for some workloads and their Pods.
652: {{< /caution >}}
653: 
654: By default, all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds. The `kubectl delete` command supports
655: the `--grace-period=<seconds>` option which allows you to override the default and specify your
656: own value.
657: 
658: Setting the grace period to `0` forcibly and immediately deletes the Pod from the API
659: server. If the Pod was still running on a node, that forcible deletion triggers the kubelet to
660: begin immediate cleanup.
661: 
662: Using kubectl, You must specify an additional flag `--force` along with `--grace-period=0`
663: in order to perform force deletions.
664: 
665: When a force deletion is performed, the API server does not wait for confirmation
666: from the kubelet that the Pod has been terminated on the node it was running on. It
667: removes the Pod in the API immediately so a new Pod can be created with the same
668: name. On the node, Pods that are set to terminate immediately will still be given
669: a small grace period before being force killed.
670: 
671: {{< caution >}}
672: Immediate deletion does not wait for confirmation that the running resource has been terminated.
673: The resource may continue to run on the cluster indefinitely.
674: {{< /caution >}}
675: 
676: If you need to force-delete Pods that are part of a StatefulSet, refer to the task
677: documentation for
678: [deleting Pods from a StatefulSet](/docs/tasks/run-application/force-delete-stateful-set-pod/).
679: 
680: ### Pod shutdown and sidecar containers {##termination-with-sidecars}
681: 
682: If your Pod includes one or more
683: [sidecar containers](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/sidecar-containers/)
684: (init containers with an Always restart policy), the kubelet will delay sending
685: the TERM signal to these sidecar containers until the last main container has fully terminated.
686: The sidecar containers will be terminated in the reverse order they are defined in the Pod spec.
687: This ensures that sidecar containers continue serving the other containers in the Pod until they
688: are no longer needed.
689: 
690: This means that slow termination of a main container will also delay the termination of the sidecar containers.
691: If the grace period expires before the termination process is complete, the Pod may enter [forced termination](#pod-termination-beyond-grace-period).
692: In this case, all remaining containers in the Pod will be terminated simultaneously with a short grace period.
693: 
694: Similarly, if the Pod has a `preStop` hook that exceeds the termination grace period, emergency termination may occur.
695: In general, if you have used `preStop` hooks to control the termination order without sidecar containers, you can now
696: remove them and allow the kubelet to manage sidecar termination automatically.
697: 
698: ### Garbage collection of Pods {#pod-garbage-collection}
699: 
700: For failed Pods, the API objects remain in the cluster's API until a human or
701: {{< glossary_tooltip term_id="controller" text="controller" >}} process
702: explicitly removes them.
703: 
704: The Pod garbage collector (PodGC), which is a controller in the control plane, cleans up
705: terminated Pods (with a phase of `Succeeded` or `Failed`), when the number of Pods exceeds the
706: configured threshold (determined by `terminated-pod-gc-threshold` in the kube-controller-manager).
707: This avoids a resource leak as Pods are created and terminated over time.
708: 
709: Additionally, PodGC cleans up any Pods which satisfy any of the following conditions:
710: 
711: 1. are orphan Pods - bound to a node which no longer exists,
712: 1. are unscheduled terminating Pods,
713: 1. are terminating Pods, bound to a non-ready node tainted with
714:    [`node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service`](/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#node-kubernetes-io-out-of-service).
715: 
716: Along with cleaning up the Pods, PodGC will also mark them as failed if they are in a non-terminal
717: phase. Also, PodGC adds a Pod disruption condition when cleaning up an orphan Pod.
718: See [Pod disruption conditions](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions#pod-disruption-conditions)
719: for more details.

67: ## Dealing with disruptions
68: 
69: Here are some ways to mitigate involuntary disruptions:
70: 
71: - Ensure your pod [requests the resources](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/assign-memory-resource) it needs.
72: - Replicate your application if you need higher availability.  (Learn about running replicated
73:   [stateless](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-stateless-application-deployment/)
74:   and [stateful](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-replicated-stateful-application/) applications.)
75: - For even higher availability when running replicated applications,
76:   spread applications across racks (using
77:   [anti-affinity](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#affinity-and-anti-affinity))
78:   or across zones (if using a
79:   [multi-zone cluster](/docs/setup/multiple-zones).)
80: 
81: The frequency of voluntary disruptions varies.  On a basic Kubernetes cluster, there are
82: no automated voluntary disruptions (only user-triggered ones).  However, your cluster administrator or hosting provider
83: may run some additional services which cause voluntary disruptions. For example,
84: rolling out node software updates can cause voluntary disruptions. Also, some implementations
85: of cluster (node) autoscaling may cause voluntary disruptions to defragment and compact nodes.
86: Your cluster administrator or hosting provider should have documented what level of voluntary
87: disruptions, if any, to expect. Certain configuration options, such as
88: [using PriorityClasses](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-priority-preemption/)
89: in your pod spec can also cause voluntary (and involuntary) disruptions.
90:

92: ## Pod disruption budgets
93: 
94: {{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.21" state="stable" >}}
95: 
96: Kubernetes offers features to help you run highly available applications even when you
97: introduce frequent voluntary disruptions.
98: 
99: As an application owner, you can create a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for each application.
100: A PDB limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from
101: voluntary disruptions. For example, a quorum-based application would
102: like to ensure that the number of replicas running is never brought below the
103: number needed for a quorum. A web front end might want to
104: ensure that the number of replicas serving load never falls below a certain
105: percentage of the total.
106: 
107: Cluster managers and hosting providers should use tools which
108: respect PodDisruptionBudgets by calling the [Eviction API](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/#eviction-api)
109: instead of directly deleting pods or deployments.
110: 
111: For example, the `kubectl drain` subcommand lets you mark a node as going out of
112: service. When you run `kubectl drain`, the tool tries to evict all of the Pods on
113: the Node you're taking out of service. The eviction request that `kubectl` submits on
114: your behalf may be temporarily rejected, so the tool periodically retries all failed
115: requests until all Pods on the target node are terminated, or until a configurable timeout
116: is reached.
117: 
118: A PDB specifies the number of replicas that an application can tolerate having, relative to how
119: many it is intended to have.  For example, a Deployment which has a `.spec.replicas: 5` is
120: supposed to have 5 pods at any given time.  If its PDB allows for there to be 4 at a time,
121: then the Eviction API will allow voluntary disruption of one (but not two) pods at a time.
122: 
123: The group of pods that comprise the application is specified using a label selector, the same
124: as the one used by the application's controller (deployment, stateful-set, etc).
125: 
126: The "intended" number of pods is computed from the `.spec.replicas` of the workload resource
127: that is managing those pods. The control plane discovers the owning workload resource by
128: examining the `.metadata.ownerReferences` of the Pod.
129: 
130: [Involuntary disruptions](#voluntary-and-involuntary-disruptions) cannot be prevented by PDBs; however they
131: do count against the budget.
132: 
133: Pods which are deleted or unavailable due to a rolling upgrade to an application do count
134: against the disruption budget, but workload resources (such as Deployment and StatefulSet)
135: are not limited by PDBs when doing rolling upgrades. Instead, the handling of failures
136: during application updates is configured in the spec for the specific workload resource.
137: 
138: It is recommended to set `AlwaysAllow` [Unhealthy Pod Eviction Policy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#unhealthy-pod-eviction-policy)
139: to your PodDisruptionBudgets to support eviction of misbehaving applications during a node drain.
140: The default behavior is to wait for the application pods to become [healthy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#healthiness-of-a-pod)
141: before the drain can proceed.
142: 
143: When a pod is evicted using the eviction API, it is gracefully
144: [terminated](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination), honoring the
145: `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting in its [PodSpec](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#podspec-v1-core).
146: 
147: ## PodDisruptionBudget example {#pdb-example}
148: 
149: Consider a cluster with 3 nodes, `node-1` through `node-3`.
150: The cluster is running several applications.  One of them has 3 replicas initially called
151: `pod-a`, `pod-b`, and `pod-c`.  Another, unrelated pod without a PDB, called `pod-x`, is also shown.
152: Initially, the pods are laid out as follows:
153: 
154: |       node-1         |       node-2        |       node-3       |
155: |:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
156: | pod-a  *available*   | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
157: | pod-x  *available*   |                     |                    |
158: 
159: All 3 pods are part of a deployment, and they collectively have a PDB which requires
160: there be at least 2 of the 3 pods to be available at all times.
161: 
162: For example, assume the cluster administrator wants to reboot into a new kernel version to fix a bug in the kernel.
163: The cluster administrator first tries to drain `node-1` using the `kubectl drain` command.
164: That tool tries to evict `pod-a` and `pod-x`.  This succeeds immediately.
165: Both pods go into the `terminating` state at the same time.
166: This puts the cluster in this state:
167: 
168: |   node-1 *draining*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
169: |:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
170: | pod-a  *terminating* | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
171: | pod-x  *terminating* |                     |                    |
172: 
173: The deployment notices that one of the pods is terminating, so it creates a replacement
174: called `pod-d`.  Since `node-1` is cordoned, it lands on another node.  Something has
175: also created `pod-y` as a replacement for `pod-x`.
176: 
177: (Note: for a StatefulSet, `pod-a`, which would be called something like `pod-0`, would need
178: to terminate completely before its replacement, which is also called `pod-0` but has a
179: different UID, could be created.  Otherwise, the example applies to a StatefulSet as well.)
180: 
181: Now the cluster is in this state:
182: 
183: |   node-1 *draining*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
184: |:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
185: | pod-a  *terminating* | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
186: | pod-x  *terminating* | pod-d *starting*    | pod-y              |

191: |:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|

49: ## How does a HorizontalPodAutoscaler work?

74: Figure 1. HorizontalPodAutoscaler controls the scale of a Deployment and its ReplicaSet
75: 
76: Kubernetes implements horizontal pod autoscaling as a control loop that runs intermittently
77: (it is not a continuous process). The interval is set by the
78: `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period` parameter to the
79: [`kube-controller-manager`](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-controller-manager/)
80: (and the default interval is 15 seconds).
81: 
82: Once during each period, the controller manager queries the resource utilization against the
83: metrics specified in each HorizontalPodAutoscaler definition. The controller manager
84: finds the target resource defined by the `scaleTargetRef`,
85: then selects the pods based on the target resource's `.spec.selector` labels,
86: and obtains the metrics from either the resource metrics API (for per-pod resource metrics),
87: or the custom metrics API (for all other metrics).
88: 
89: - For per-pod resource metrics (like CPU), the controller fetches the metrics
90:   from the resource metrics API for each Pod targeted by the HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
91:   Then, if a target utilization value is set, the controller calculates the utilization
92:   value as a percentage of the equivalent
93:   [resource request](/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/#requests-and-limits)
94:   on the containers in each Pod. If a target raw value is set, the raw metric values are used directly.
95:   The controller then takes the mean of the utilization or the raw value (depending on the type
96:   of target specified) across all targeted Pods, and produces a ratio used to scale
97:   the number of desired replicas.
98: 
99:   Please note that if some of the Pod's containers do not have the relevant resource request set,
100:   CPU utilization for the Pod will not be defined and the autoscaler will
101:   not take any action for that metric. See the [algorithm details](#algorithm-details) section below
102:   for more information about how the autoscaling algorithm works.
103: 
104: - For per-pod custom metrics, the controller functions similarly to per-pod resource metrics,
105:   except that it works with raw values, not utilization values.
106: 
107: - For object metrics and external metrics, a single metric is fetched, which describes
108:   the object in question. This metric is compared to the target
109:   value, to produce a ratio as above. In the `autoscaling/v2` API
110:   version, this value can optionally be divided by the number of Pods before the
111:   comparison is made.
112: 
113: The common use for HorizontalPodAutoscaler is to configure it to fetch metrics from
114: {{< glossary_tooltip text="aggregated APIs" term_id="aggregation-layer" >}}
115: (`metrics.k8s.io`, `custom.metrics.k8s.io`, or `external.metrics.k8s.io`). The `metrics.k8s.io` API is
116: usually provided by an add-on named Metrics Server, which needs to be launched separately.
117: For more information about resource metrics, see
118: [Metrics Server](/docs/tasks/debug/debug-cluster/resource-metrics-pipeline/#metrics-server).
119: 
120: [Support for metrics APIs](#support-for-metrics-apis) explains the stability guarantees and support status for these
121: different APIs.
122: 
123: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller accesses corresponding workload resources that support scaling (such as Deployments
124: and StatefulSet). These resources each have a subresource named `scale`, an interface that allows you to dynamically set the
125: number of replicas and examine each of their current states.
126: For general information about subresources in the Kubernetes API, see
127: [Kubernetes API Concepts](/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/).
128: 
129: ### Algorithm details
130: 
131: From the most basic perspective, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
132: operates on the ratio between desired metric value and current metric
133: value:
134: 
135: ```math
136: \begin{equation*}
137: desiredReplicas = ceil\left\lceil currentReplicas \times \frac{currentMetricValue}{desiredMetricValue} \right\rceil
138: \end{equation*}
139: ```
140: 
141: For example, if the current metric value is `200m`, and the desired value
142: is `100m`, the number of replicas will be doubled, since
143: \\( { 200.0 \div 100.0 } = 2.0 \\).  
144: If the current value is instead `50m`, you'll halve the number of
145: replicas, since \\( { 50.0 \div 100.0 } = 0.5 \\). The control plane skips any scaling
146: action if the ratio is sufficiently close to 1.0 (within a globally-configurable
147: tolerance, 0.1 by default).
148: 
149: When a `targetAverageValue` or `targetAverageUtilization` is specified,
150: the `currentMetricValue` is computed by taking the average of the given
151: metric across all Pods in the HorizontalPodAutoscaler's scale target.
152: 
153: Before checking the tolerance and deciding on the final values, the control
154: plane also considers whether any metrics are missing, and how many Pods
155: are [`Ready`](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-conditions).
156: All Pods with a deletion timestamp set (objects with a deletion timestamp are
157: in the process of being shut down / removed) are ignored, and all failed Pods
158: are discarded.
159: 
160: If a particular Pod is missing metrics, it is set aside for later; Pods
161: with missing metrics will be used to adjust the final scaling amount.
162: 
163: When scaling on CPU, if any pod has yet to become ready (it's still
164: initializing, or possibly is unhealthy) _or_ the most recent metric point for
165: the pod was before it became ready, that pod is set aside as well.
166: 
167: Due to technical constraints, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
168: cannot exactly determine the first time a pod becomes ready when
169: determining whether to set aside certain CPU metrics. Instead, it
170: considers a Pod "not yet ready" if it's unready and transitioned to
171: ready within a short, configurable window of time since it started.
172: This value is configured with the `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-initial-readiness-delay`
173: flag, and its default is 30 seconds.
174: Once a pod has become ready, it considers any transition to
175: ready to be the first if it occurred within a longer, configurable time
176: since it started. This value is configured with the
177: `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-cpu-initialization-period` flag, and its
178: default is 5 minutes.
179: 
180: The \\( currentMetricValue \over desiredMetricValue \\) base scale ratio is then
181: calculated, using the remaining pods not set aside or discarded from above.
182: 
183: If there were any missing metrics, the control plane recomputes the average more
184: conservatively, assuming those pods were consuming 100% of the desired
185: value in case of a scale down, and 0% in case of a scale up. This dampens
186: the magnitude of any potential scale.
187: 
188: Furthermore, if any not-yet-ready pods were present, and the workload would have
189: scaled up without factoring in missing metrics or not-yet-ready pods,
190: the controller conservatively assumes that the not-yet-ready pods are consuming 0%
191: of the desired metric, further dampening the magnitude of a scale up.
192: 
193: After factoring in the not-yet-ready pods and missing metrics, the
194: controller recalculates the usage ratio. If the new ratio reverses the scale
195: direction, or is within the tolerance, the controller doesn't take any scaling
196: action. In other cases, the new ratio is used to decide any change to the
197: number of Pods.
198: 
199: Note that the _original_ value for the average utilization is reported
200: back via the HorizontalPodAutoscaler status, without factoring in the
201: not-yet-ready pods or missing metrics, even when the new usage ratio is
202: used.
203: 
204: If multiple metrics are specified in a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, this
205: calculation is done for each metric, and then the largest of the desired
206: replica counts is chosen. If any of these metrics cannot be converted
207: into a desired replica count (e.g. due to an error fetching the metrics
208: from the metrics APIs) and a scale down is suggested by the metrics which
209: can be fetched, scaling is skipped. This means that the HPA is still capable
210: of scaling up if one or more metrics give a `desiredReplicas` greater than
211: the current value.
212: 
213: Finally, right before HPA scales the target, the scale recommendation is recorded. The
214: controller considers all recommendations within a configurable window choosing the
215: highest recommendation from within that window. This value can be configured using the
216: `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-downscale-stabilization` flag, which defaults to 5 minutes.
217: This means that scaledowns will occur gradually, smoothing out the impact of rapidly
218: fluctuating metric values.
219: 
220: ## API Object
221: 
222: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is an API resource in the Kubernetes
223: `autoscaling` API group. The current stable version can be found in
224: the `autoscaling/v2` API version which includes support for scaling on
225: memory and custom metrics. The new fields introduced in
226: `autoscaling/v2` are preserved as annotations when working with
227: `autoscaling/v1`.
228: 
229: When you create a HorizontalPodAutoscaler API object, make sure the name specified is a valid
230: [DNS subdomain name](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/names#dns-subdomain-names).
231: More details about the API object can be found at
232: [HorizontalPodAutoscaler Object](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#horizontalpodautoscaler-v2-autoscaling).
233: 
234: ## Stability of workload scale {#flapping}
235: 
236: When managing the scale of a group of replicas using the HorizontalPodAutoscaler,
237: it is possible that the number of replicas keeps fluctuating frequently due to the
238: dynamic nature of the metrics evaluated. This is sometimes referred to as _thrashing_,
239: or _flapping_. It's similar to the concept of _hysteresis_ in cybernetics.

580: ## Comparison with podAffinity and podAntiAffinity {#comparison-with-podaffinity-podantiaffinity}
581: 
582: In Kubernetes, [inter-Pod affinity and anti-affinity](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#inter-pod-affinity-and-anti-affinity)
583: control how Pods are scheduled in relation to one another - either more packed
584: or more scattered.
585: 
586: `podAffinity`
587: : attracts Pods; you can try to pack any number of Pods into qualifying
588:   topology domain(s).
589: 
590: `podAntiAffinity`
591: : repels Pods. If you set this to `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` mode then
592:   only a single Pod can be scheduled into a single topology domain; if you choose
593:   `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` then you lose the ability to enforce the
594:   constraint.
595: 
596: For finer control, you can specify topology spread constraints to distribute
597: Pods across different topology domains - to achieve either high availability or
598: cost-saving. This can also help on rolling update workloads and scaling out
599: replicas smoothly.
600: 
601: For more context, see the
602: [Motivation](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/895-pod-topology-spread#motivation)
603: section of the enhancement proposal about Pod topology spread constraints.
604:

606: 
607: - There's no guarantee that the constraints remain satisfied when Pods are removed. For
608:   example, scaling down a Deployment may result in imbalanced Pods distribution.
609: 
610:   You can use a tool such as the [Descheduler](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/descheduler)
611:   to rebalance the Pods distribution.
612: - Pods matched on tainted nodes are respected.
613:   See [Issue 80921](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/80921).
614: - The scheduler doesn't have prior knowledge of all the zones or other topology
615:   domains that a cluster has. They are determined from the existing nodes in the
616:   cluster. This could lead to a problem in autoscaled clusters, when a node pool (or
617:   node group) is scaled to zero nodes, and you're expecting the cluster to scale up,
618:   because, in this case, those topology domains won't be considered until there is
619:   at least one node in them.
620: 
621:   You can work around this by using a Node autoscaler that is aware of
622:   Pod topology spread constraints and is also aware of the overall set of topology
623:   domains.

27: ## Requests and limits
28: 
29: If the node where a Pod is running has enough of a resource available, it's possible (and
30: allowed) for a container to use more resource than its `request` for that resource specifies.
31: 
32: For example, if you set a `memory` request of 256 MiB for a container, and that container is in
33: a Pod scheduled to a Node with 8GiB of memory and no other Pods, then the container can try to use
34: more RAM.
35: 
36: Limits are a different story. Both `cpu` and `memory` limits are applied by the kubelet (and
37: {{< glossary_tooltip text="container runtime" term_id="container-runtime" >}}),
38: and are ultimately enforced by the kernel. On Linux nodes, the Linux kernel
39: enforces limits with
40: {{< glossary_tooltip text="cgroups" term_id="cgroup" >}}.
41: The behavior of `cpu` and `memory` limit enforcement is slightly different.
42: 
43: `cpu` limits are enforced by CPU throttling. When a container approaches
44: its `cpu` limit, the kernel will restrict access to the CPU corresponding to the
45: container's limit. Thus, a `cpu` limit is a hard limit the kernel enforces.
46: Containers may not use more CPU than is specified in their `cpu` limit.
47: 
48: `memory` limits are enforced by the kernel with out of memory (OOM) kills. When
49: a container uses more than its `memory` limit, the kernel may terminate it. However,
50: terminations only happen when the kernel detects memory pressure. Thus, a
51: container that over allocates memory may not be immediately killed. This means
52: `memory` limits are enforced reactively. A container may use more memory than
53: its `memory` limit, but if it does, it may get killed.
54: 
55: {{< note >}}
56: There is an alpha feature `MemoryQoS` which attempts to add more preemptive
57: limit enforcement for memory (as opposed to reactive enforcement by the OOM
58: killer). However, this effort is
59: [stalled](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/a47155b340/keps/sig-node/2570-memory-qos#latest-update-stalled)

64: If you specify a limit for a resource, but do not specify any request, and no admission-time
65: mechanism has applied a default request for that resource, then Kubernetes copies the limit
66: you specified and uses it as the requested value for the resource.
67: {{< /note >}}
68: 
69: ## Resource types
70: 
71: *CPU* and *memory* are each a *resource type*. A resource type has a base unit.
72: CPU represents compute processing and is specified in units of [Kubernetes CPUs](#meaning-of-cpu).
73: Memory is specified in units of bytes.
74: For Linux workloads, you can specify _huge page_ resources.
75: Huge pages are a Linux-specific feature where the node kernel allocates blocks of memory
76: that are much larger than the default page size.
77: 
78: For example, on a system where the default page size is 4KiB, you could specify a limit,
79: `hugepages-2Mi: 80Mi`. If the container tries allocating over 40 2MiB huge pages (a
80: total of 80 MiB), that allocation fails.
81: 
82: {{< note >}}
83: You cannot overcommit `hugepages-*` resources.
84: This is different from the `memory` and `cpu` resources.
85: {{< /note >}}
86: 
87: CPU and memory are collectively referred to as *compute resources*, or *resources*. Compute
88: resources are measurable quantities that can be requested, allocated, and
89: consumed. They are distinct from
90: [API resources](/docs/concepts/overview/kubernetes-api/). API resources, such as Pods and
91: [Services](/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/) are objects that can be read and modified
92: through the Kubernetes API server.
93: 
94: ## Resource requests and limits of Pod and container
95: 
96: For each container, you can specify resource limits and requests,
97: including the following:
98: 
99: * `spec.containers[].resources.limits.cpu`
100: * `spec.containers[].resources.limits.memory`
101: * `spec.containers[].resources.limits.hugepages-<size>`
102: * `spec.containers[].resources.requests.cpu`
103: * `spec.containers[].resources.requests.memory`
104: * `spec.containers[].resources.requests.hugepages-<size>`
105: 
106: Although you can only specify requests and limits for individual containers,
107: it is also useful to think about the overall resource requests and limits for
108: a Pod.
109: For a particular resource, a *Pod resource request/limit* is the sum of the
110: resource requests/limits of that type for each container in the Pod.
111: 
112: ## Pod-level resource specification
113: 
114: {{< feature-state feature_gate_name="PodLevelResources" >}}
115: 
116: Starting in Kubernetes 1.32, you can also specify resource requests and limits at
117: the Pod level. At the Pod level, Kubernetes {{< skew currentVersion >}}
118: only supports resource requests or limits for specific resource types: `cpu` and /
119: or `memory`. This feature is currently in alpha and with the feature enabled,
120: Kubernetes allows you to declare an overall resource budget for the Pod, which is
121: especially helpful when dealing with a large number of containers where it can be
122: difficult to accurately gauge individual resource needs. Additionally, it enables
123: containers within a Pod to share idle resources with each other, improving resource
124: utilization. 
125: 
126: For a Pod, you can specify resource limits and requests for CPU and memory by including the following:
127: * `spec.resources.limits.cpu`
128: * `spec.resources.limits.memory`
129: * `spec.resources.requests.cpu`
130: * `spec.resources.requests.memory`
131: 
132: ## Resource units in Kubernetes
133: 
134: ### CPU resource units {#meaning-of-cpu}
135: 
136: Limits and requests for CPU resources are measured in *cpu* units.
137: In Kubernetes, 1 CPU unit is equivalent to **1 physical CPU core**,
138: or **1 virtual core**, depending on whether the node is a physical host
139: or a virtual machine running inside a physical machine.
140: 
141: Fractional requests are allowed. When you define a container with
142: `spec.containers[].resources.requests.cpu` set to `0.5`, you are requesting half
143: as much CPU time compared to if you asked for `1.0` CPU.
144: For CPU resource units, the [quantity](/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/common-definitions/quantity/) expression `0.1` is equivalent to the
145: expression `100m`, which can be read as "one hundred millicpu". Some people say
146: "one hundred millicores", and this is understood to mean the same thing.
147: 
148: CPU resource is always specified as an absolute amount of resource, never as a relative amount. For example,
149: `500m` CPU represents the roughly same amount of computing power whether that container
150: runs on a single-core, dual-core, or 48-core machine.
151: 
152: {{< note >}}
153: Kubernetes doesn't allow you to specify CPU resources with a precision finer than
154: `1m` or `0.001` CPU. To avoid accidentally using an invalid CPU quantity, it's useful to specify CPU units using the milliCPU form 
155: instead of the decimal form when using less than 1 CPU unit. 
156: 
157: For example, you have a Pod that uses `5m` or `0.005` CPU and would like to decrease
158: its CPU resources. By using the decimal form, it's harder to spot that `0.0005` CPU
159: is an invalid value, while by using the milliCPU form, it's easier to spot that
160: `0.5m` is an invalid value.
161: {{< /note >}}
162: 
163: ### Memory resource units {#meaning-of-memory}
164: 
165: Limits and requests for `memory` are measured in bytes. You can express memory as
166: a plain integer or as a fixed-point number using one of these
167: [quantity](/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/common-definitions/quantity/) suffixes:
168: E, P, T, G, M, k. You can also use the power-of-two equivalents: Ei, Pi, Ti, Gi,
169: Mi, Ki. For example, the following represent roughly the same value:
170: 
171: ```shell
172: 128974848, 129e6, 129M,  128974848000m, 123Mi
173: ```
174: 
175: Pay attention to the case of the suffixes. If you request `400m` of memory, this is a request
176: for 0.4 bytes. Someone who types that probably meant to ask for 400 mebibytes (`400Mi`)
177: or 400 megabytes (`400M`).
178: 
179: ## Container resources example {#example-1}
180: 
181: The following Pod has two containers. Both containers are defined with a request for
182: 0.25 CPU
183: and 64MiB (2<sup>26</sup> bytes) of memory. Each container has a limit of 0.5
184: CPU and 128MiB of memory. You can say the Pod has a request of 0.5 CPU and 128
185: MiB of memory, and a limit of 1 CPU and 256MiB of memory.
186: 
187: ```yaml
188: ---
189: apiVersion: v1
190: kind: Pod
191: metadata:
192:   name: frontend
193: spec:
194:   containers:
195:   - name: app
196:     image: images.my-company.example/app:v4
197:     resources:
198:       requests:
199:         memory: "64Mi"
200:         cpu: "250m"
201:       limits:
202:         memory: "128Mi"
203:         cpu: "500m"
204:   - name: log-aggregator
205:     image: images.my-company.example/log-aggregator:v6
206:     resources:
207:       requests:
208:         memory: "64Mi"
209:         cpu: "250m"
210:       limits:
211:         memory: "128Mi"
212:         cpu: "500m"
213: ```

21: If you want to control traffic flow at the IP address or port level for TCP, UDP, and SCTP protocols,
22: then you might consider using Kubernetes NetworkPolicies for particular applications in your cluster.
23: NetworkPolicies are an application-centric construct which allow you to specify how a
24: {{< glossary_tooltip text="pod" term_id="pod">}} is allowed to communicate with various network
25: "entities" (we use the word "entity" here to avoid overloading the more common terms such as
26: "endpoints" and "services", which have specific Kubernetes connotations) over the network.
27: NetworkPolicies apply to a connection with a pod on one or both ends, and are not relevant to
28: other connections.
29: 
30: The entities that a Pod can communicate with are identified through a combination of the following
31: three identifiers:
32: 
33: 1. Other pods that are allowed (exception: a pod cannot block access to itself)
34: 1. Namespaces that are allowed
35: 1. IP blocks (exception: traffic to and from the node where a Pod is running is always allowed,
36:    regardless of the IP address of the Pod or the node)
37: 
38: When defining a pod- or namespace-based NetworkPolicy, you use a
39: {{< glossary_tooltip text="selector" term_id="selector">}} to specify what traffic is allowed to
40: and from the Pod(s) that match the selector.
41: 
42: Meanwhile, when IP-based NetworkPolicies are created, we define policies based on IP blocks (CIDR ranges).
43: 
44: <!-- body -->
45: ## Prerequisites
46: 
47: Network policies are implemented by the [network plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/network-plugins/).
48: To use network policies, you must be using a networking solution which supports NetworkPolicy.
49: Creating a NetworkPolicy resource without a controller that implements it will have no effect.
50: 
51: ## The two sorts of pod isolation
52: 
53: There are two sorts of isolation for a pod: isolation for egress, and isolation for ingress.
54: They concern what connections may be established. "Isolation" here is not absolute, rather it
55: means "some restrictions apply". The alternative, "non-isolated for $direction", means that no
56: restrictions apply in the stated direction. The two sorts of isolation (or not) are declared
57: independently, and are both relevant for a connection from one pod to another.
58: 
59: By default, a pod is non-isolated for egress; all outbound connections are allowed.
60: A pod is isolated for egress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and has
61: "Egress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for egress.
62: When a pod is isolated for egress, the only allowed connections from the pod are those allowed by
63: the `egress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to the pod for egress. Reply traffic for those
64: allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
65: The effects of those `egress` lists combine additively.
66: 
67: By default, a pod is non-isolated for ingress; all inbound connections are allowed.
68: A pod is isolated for ingress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and
69: has "Ingress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for ingress.
70: When a pod is isolated for ingress, the only allowed connections into the pod are those from
71: the pod's node and those allowed by the `ingress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to
72: the pod for ingress. Reply traffic for those allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
73: The effects of those `ingress` lists combine additively.
74: 
75: Network policies do not conflict; they are additive. If any policy or policies apply to a given
76: pod for a given direction, the connections allowed in that direction from that pod is the union of
77: what the applicable policies allow. Thus, order of evaluation does not affect the policy result.
78: 
79: For a connection from a source pod to a destination pod to be allowed, both the egress policy on
80: the source pod and the ingress policy on the destination pod need to allow the connection. If
81: either side does not allow the connection, it will not happen.
82: 
83: ## The NetworkPolicy resource {#networkpolicy-resource}
84: 
85: See the [NetworkPolicy](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#networkpolicy-v1-networking-k8s-io)
86: reference for a full definition of the resource.
87: 
88: An example NetworkPolicy might look like this:
89: 
90: {{% code_sample file="service/networking/networkpolicy.yaml" %}}
91: 
92: {{< note >}}
93: POSTing this to the API server for your cluster will have no effect unless your chosen networking
94: solution supports network policy.
95: {{< /note >}}
96: 
97: __Mandatory Fields__: As with all other Kubernetes config, a NetworkPolicy needs `apiVersion`,
98: `kind`, and `metadata` fields. For general information about working with config files, see
99: [Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-pod-configmap/),
100: and [Object Management](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/object-management).
101: 
102: **spec**: NetworkPolicy [spec](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#spec-and-status)
103: has all the information needed to define a particular network policy in the given namespace.
104: 
105: **podSelector**: Each NetworkPolicy includes a `podSelector` which selects the grouping of pods to
106: which the policy applies. The example policy selects pods with the label "role=db". An empty
107: `podSelector` selects all pods in the namespace.
108: 
109: **policyTypes**: Each NetworkPolicy includes a `policyTypes` list which may include either
110: `Ingress`, `Egress`, or both. The `policyTypes` field indicates whether or not the given policy
111: applies to ingress traffic to selected pod, egress traffic from selected pods, or both. If no
112: `policyTypes` are specified on a NetworkPolicy then by default `Ingress` will always be set and
113: `Egress` will be set if the NetworkPolicy has any egress rules.
114: 
115: **ingress**: Each NetworkPolicy may include a list of allowed `ingress` rules. Each rule allows
116: traffic which matches both the `from` and `ports` sections. The example policy contains a single
117: rule, which matches traffic on a single port, from one of three sources, the first specified via
118: an `ipBlock`, the second via a `namespaceSelector` and the third via a `podSelector`.
119: 
120: **egress**: Each NetworkPolicy may include a list of allowed `egress` rules. Each rule allows
121: traffic which matches both the `to` and `ports` sections. The example policy contains a single
122: rule, which matches traffic on a single port to any destination in `10.0.0.0/24`.
123: 
124: So, the example NetworkPolicy:
125: 
126: 1. isolates `role=db` pods in the `default` namespace for both ingress and egress traffic
127:    (if they weren't already isolated)
128: 1. (Ingress rules) allows connections to all pods in the `default` namespace with the label
129:    `role=db` on TCP port 6379 from:
130: 
131:    * any pod in the `default` namespace with the label `role=frontend`
132:    * any pod in a namespace with the label `project=myproject`
133:    * IP addresses in the ranges `172.17.0.0`–`172.17.0.255` and `172.17.2.0`–`172.17.255.255`
134:      (ie, all of `172.17.0.0/16` except `172.17.1.0/24`)
135: 
136: 1. (Egress rules) allows connections from any pod in the `default` namespace with the label
137:    `role=db` to CIDR `10.0.0.0/24` on TCP port 5978
138: 
139: See the [Declare Network Policy](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/declare-network-policy/)
140: walkthrough for further examples.
141: 
142: ## Behavior of `to` and `from` selectors
143: 
144: There are four kinds of selectors that can be specified in an `ingress` `from` section or `egress`
145: `to` section:
146: 
147: **podSelector**: This selects particular Pods in the same namespace as the NetworkPolicy which
148: should be allowed as ingress sources or egress destinations.

391: The optional `.spec.persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` field controls if
392: and how PVCs are deleted during the lifecycle of a StatefulSet. You must enable the
393: `StatefulSetAutoDeletePVC` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/)
394: on the API server and the controller manager to use this field. 
395: Once enabled, there are two policies you can configure for each StatefulSet:
396: 
397: `whenDeleted`
398: : configures the volume retention behavior that applies when the StatefulSet is deleted
399: 
400: `whenScaled`
401: : configures the volume retention behavior that applies when the replica count of
402:   the StatefulSet   is reduced; for example, when scaling down the set.
403:   
404: For each policy that you can configure, you can set the value to either `Delete` or `Retain`.
405: 
406: `Delete`
407: : The PVCs created from the StatefulSet `volumeClaimTemplate` are deleted for each Pod
408:   affected by the policy. With the `whenDeleted` policy all PVCs from the
409:   `volumeClaimTemplate` are deleted after their Pods have been deleted. With the
410:   `whenScaled` policy, only PVCs corresponding to Pod replicas being scaled down are
411:   deleted, after their Pods have been deleted.
412: 
413: `Retain` (default)
414: : PVCs from the `volumeClaimTemplate` are not affected when their Pod is
415:   deleted. This is the behavior before this new feature.
416: 
417: Bear in mind that these policies **only** apply when Pods are being removed due to the
418: StatefulSet being deleted or scaled down. For example, if a Pod associated with a StatefulSet
419: fails due to node failure, and the control plane creates a replacement Pod, the StatefulSet
420: retains the existing PVC.  The existing volume is unaffected, and the cluster will attach it to
421: the node where the new Pod is about to launch.
422:   
423: The default for policies is `Retain`, matching the StatefulSet behavior before this new feature.
424: 
425: Here is an example policy.
426: 
427: ```yaml
428: apiVersion: apps/v1
429: kind: StatefulSet
430: ...
431: spec:
432:   persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
433:     whenDeleted: Retain
434:     whenScaled: Delete
435: ...
436: ```
437: 
438: The StatefulSet {{<glossary_tooltip text="controller" term_id="controller">}} adds
439: [owner references](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/owners-dependents/#owner-references-in-object-specifications)
440: to its PVCs, which are then deleted by the {{<glossary_tooltip text="garbage collector"
441: term_id="garbage-collection">}} after the Pod is terminated. This enables the Pod to
442: cleanly unmount all volumes before the PVCs are deleted (and before the backing PV and
443: volume are deleted, depending on the retain policy).  When you set the `whenDeleted`
444: policy to `Delete`, an owner reference to the StatefulSet instance is placed on all PVCs
445: associated with that StatefulSet.
446: 
447: The `whenScaled` policy must delete PVCs only when a Pod is scaled down, and not when a
448: Pod is deleted for another reason. When reconciling, the StatefulSet controller compares
449: its desired replica count to the actual Pods present on the cluster. Any StatefulSet Pod
450: whose id greater than the replica count is condemned and marked for deletion. If the
451: `whenScaled` policy is `Delete`, the condemned Pods are first set as owners to the
452: associated StatefulSet template PVCs, before the Pod is deleted. This causes the PVCs
453: to be garbage collected after only the condemned Pods have terminated.
454: 
455: This means that if the controller crashes and restarts, no Pod will be deleted before its
456: owner reference has been updated appropriate to the policy. If a condemned Pod is
457: force-deleted while the controller is down, the owner reference may or may not have been
458: set up, depending on when the controller crashed. It may take several reconcile loops to
459: update the owner references, so some condemned Pods may have set up owner references and
460: others may not. For this reason we recommend waiting for the controller to come back up,
461: which will verify owner references before terminating Pods. If that is not possible, the
462: operator should verify the owner references on PVCs to ensure the expected objects are
463: deleted when Pods are force-deleted.
464: 
465: ### Replicas
466: 
467: `.spec.replicas` is an optional field that specifies the number of desired Pods. It defaults to 1.
468: 
469: Should you manually scale a deployment, example via `kubectl scale
470: statefulset statefulset --replicas=X`, and then you update that StatefulSet
471: based on a manifest (for example: by running `kubectl apply -f
472: statefulset.yaml`), then applying that manifest overwrites the manual scaling
473: that you previously did.

1166: `.spec.strategy` specifies the strategy used to replace old Pods by new ones.

1185: The Deployment updates Pods in a rolling update

1194: rounding down. The value cannot be 0 if `.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge` is 0. The default value is 25%.
