178: ### Reclaiming
179: 
180: When a user is done with their volume, they can delete the PVC objects from the
181: API that allows reclamation of the resource. The reclaim policy for a PersistentVolume
182: tells the cluster what to do with the volume after it has been released of its claim.
183: Currently, volumes can either be Retained, Recycled, or Deleted.
184: 
185: #### Retain
186: 
187: The `Retain` reclaim policy allows for manual reclamation of the resource.
188: When the PersistentVolumeClaim is deleted, the PersistentVolume still exists
189: and the volume is considered "released". But it is not yet available for
190: another claim because the previous claimant's data remains on the volume.
191: An administrator can manually reclaim the volume with the following steps.
192: 
193: 1. Delete the PersistentVolume. The associated storage asset in external infrastructure
194:    still exists after the PV is deleted.
195: 1. Manually clean up the data on the associated storage asset accordingly.
196: 1. Manually delete the associated storage asset.
197: 
198: If you want to reuse the same storage asset, create a new PersistentVolume with
199: the same storage asset definition.
200: 
201: #### Delete
202: 
203: For volume plugins that support the `Delete` reclaim policy, deletion removes
204: both the PersistentVolume object from Kubernetes, as well as the associated
205: storage asset in the external infrastructure. Volumes that were dynamically provisioned
206: inherit the [reclaim policy of their StorageClass](#reclaim-policy), which
207: defaults to `Delete`. The administrator should configure the StorageClass
208: according to users' expectations; otherwise, the PV must be edited or
209: patched after it is created. See
210: [Change the Reclaim Policy of a PersistentVolume](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/change-pv-reclaim-policy/).
211: 
212: #### Recycle
213: 
214: {{< warning >}}
215: The `Recycle` reclaim policy is deprecated. Instead, the recommended approach
216: is to use dynamic provisioning.
217: {{< /warning >}}
218: 
219: If supported by the underlying volume plugin, the `Recycle` reclaim policy performs
220: a basic scrub (`rm -rf /thevolume/*`) on the volume and makes it available again for a new claim.
221: 
222: However, an administrator can configure a custom recycler Pod template using
223: the Kubernetes controller manager command line arguments as described in the
224: [reference](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-controller-manager/).
225: The custom recycler Pod template must contain a `volumes` specification, as
226: shown in the example below:
227: 
228: ```yaml
229: apiVersion: v1
230: kind: Pod
231: metadata:
232:   name: pv-recycler
233:   namespace: default
234: spec:
235:   restartPolicy: Never
236:   volumes:
237:   - name: vol
238:     hostPath:
239:       path: /any/path/it/will/be/replaced
240:   containers:
241:   - name: pv-recycler
242:     image: "registry.k8s.io/busybox"
243:     command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "test -e /scrub && rm -rf /scrub/..?* /scrub/.[!.]* /scrub/*  && test -z \"$(ls -A /scrub)\" || exit 1"]
244:     volumeMounts:
245:     - name: vol
246:       mountPath: /scrub
247: ```
248: 
249: However, the particular path specified in the custom recycler Pod template in the
250: `volumes` part is replaced with the particular path of the volume that is being recycled.
251:

253: {{< feature-state feature_gate_name="HonorPVReclaimPolicy" >}}

259: in  v1.31) is added to both dynamically provisioned and statically provisioned

349: ## Define readiness probes
350: 
351: Sometimes, applications are temporarily unable to serve traffic.
352: For example, an application might need to load large data or configuration
353: files during startup, or depend on external services after startup.
354: In such cases, you don't want to kill the application,
355: but you don't want to send it requests either. Kubernetes provides
356: readiness probes to detect and mitigate these situations. A pod with containers
357: reporting that they are not ready does not receive traffic through Kubernetes
358: Services.
359: 
360: {{< note >}}
361: Readiness probes runs on the container during its whole lifecycle.
362: {{< /note >}}
363: 
364: {{< caution >}}
365: The readiness and liveness probes do not depend on each other to succeed.
366: If you want to wait before executing a readiness probe, you should use
367: `initialDelaySeconds` or a `startupProbe`.
368: {{< /caution >}}
369: 
370: Readiness probes are configured similarly to liveness probes. The only difference
371: is that you use the `readinessProbe` field instead of the `livenessProbe` field.
372: 
373: ```yaml
374: readinessProbe:
375:   exec:
376:     command:
377:     - cat
378:     - /tmp/healthy
379:   initialDelaySeconds: 5
380:   periodSeconds: 5
381: ```
382: 
383: Configuration for HTTP and TCP readiness probes also remains identical to
384: liveness probes.
385: 
386: Readiness and liveness probes can be used in parallel for the same container.
387: Using both can ensure that traffic does not reach a container that is not ready
388: for it, and that containers are restarted when they fail.
389: 
390: ## Configure Probes
391: 
392: <!--Eventually, some of this section could be moved to a concept topic.-->
393: 
394: [Probes](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#probe-v1-core)
395: have a number of fields that you can use to more precisely control the behavior of startup,
396: liveness and readiness checks:
397: 
398: * `initialDelaySeconds`: Number of seconds after the container has started before startup,
399:   liveness or readiness probes are initiated. If a startup  probe is defined, liveness and
400:   readiness probe delays do not begin until the startup probe has succeeded. If the value of
401:   `periodSeconds` is greater than `initialDelaySeconds` then the `initialDelaySeconds` will be
402:   ignored. Defaults to 0 seconds. Minimum value is 0.
403: * `periodSeconds`: How often (in seconds) to perform the probe. Default to 10 seconds.
404:   The minimum value is 1.
405:   While a container is not Ready, the `ReadinessProbe` may be executed at times other than
406:   the configured `periodSeconds` interval. This is to make the Pod ready faster.
407: * `timeoutSeconds`: Number of seconds after which the probe times out.
408:   Defaults to 1 second. Minimum value is 1.
409: * `successThreshold`: Minimum consecutive successes for the probe to be considered successful
410:   after having failed. Defaults to 1. Must be 1 for liveness and startup Probes.
411:   Minimum value is 1.
412: * `failureThreshold`: After a probe fails `failureThreshold` times in a row, Kubernetes
413:   considers that the overall check has failed: the container is _not_ ready/healthy/live.
414:   Defaults to 3. Minimum value is 1.
415:   For the case of a startup or liveness probe, if at least `failureThreshold` probes have
416:   failed, Kubernetes treats the container as unhealthy and triggers a restart for that
417:   specific container. The kubelet honors the setting of `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`
418:   for that container.
419:   For a failed readiness probe, the kubelet continues running the container that failed
420:   checks, and also continues to run more probes; because the check failed, the kubelet
421:   sets the `Ready` [condition](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-conditions)
422:   on the Pod to `false`.
423: * `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`: configure a grace period for the kubelet to wait between
424:   triggering a shut down of the failed container, and then forcing the container runtime to stop
425:   that container.
426:   The default is to inherit the Pod-level value for `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`
427:   (30 seconds if not specified), and the minimum value is 1.
428:   See [probe-level `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`](#probe-level-terminationgraceperiodseconds)
429:   for more detail.
430:

432: Incorrect implementation of readiness probes may result in an ever growing number
433: of processes in the container, and resource starvation if this is left unchecked.
434: {{< /caution >}}

230: ## How Pods with resource requests are scheduled
231: 
232: When you create a Pod, the Kubernetes scheduler selects a node for the Pod to
233: run on. Each node has a maximum capacity for each of the resource types: the
234: amount of CPU and memory it can provide for Pods. The scheduler ensures that,
235: for each resource type, the sum of the resource requests of the scheduled
236: containers is less than the capacity of the node.
237: Note that although actual memory
238: or CPU resource usage on nodes is very low, the scheduler still refuses to place
239: a Pod on a node if the capacity check fails. This protects against a resource
240: shortage on a node when resource usage later increases, for example, during a
241: daily peak in request rate.
242: 
243: ## How Kubernetes applies resource requests and limits {#how-pods-with-resource-limits-are-run}
244: 
245: When the kubelet starts a container as part of a Pod, the kubelet passes that container's
246: requests and limits for memory and CPU to the container runtime.
247: 
248: On Linux, the container runtime typically configures
249: kernel {{< glossary_tooltip text="cgroups" term_id="cgroup" >}} that apply and enforce the
250: limits you defined.
251: 
252: - The CPU limit defines a hard ceiling on how much CPU time the container can use.
253:   During each scheduling interval (time slice), the Linux kernel checks to see if this
254:   limit is exceeded; if so, the kernel waits before allowing that cgroup to resume execution.
255: - The CPU request typically defines a weighting. If several different containers (cgroups)
256:   want to run on a contended system, workloads with larger CPU requests are allocated more
257:   CPU time than workloads with small requests.
258: - The memory request is mainly used during (Kubernetes) Pod scheduling. On a node that uses
259:   cgroups v2, the container runtime might use the memory request as a hint to set
260:   `memory.min` and `memory.low`.
261: - The memory limit defines a memory limit for that cgroup. If the container tries to
262:   allocate more memory than this limit, the Linux kernel out-of-memory subsystem activates
263:   and, typically, intervenes by stopping one of the processes in the container that tried
264:   to allocate memory. If that process is the container's PID 1, and the container is marked
265:   as restartable, Kubernetes restarts the container.
266: - The memory limit for the Pod or container can also apply to pages in memory backed
267:   volumes, such as an `emptyDir`. The kubelet tracks `tmpfs` emptyDir volumes as container
268:   memory use, rather than as local ephemeral storage.　When using memory backed `emptyDir`,
269:   be sure to check the notes [below](#memory-backed-emptydir).
270: 
271: If a container exceeds its memory request and the node that it runs on becomes short of
272: memory overall, it is likely that the Pod the container belongs to will be
273: {{< glossary_tooltip text="evicted" term_id="eviction" >}}.
274: 
275: A container might or might not be allowed to exceed its CPU limit for extended periods of time.
276: However, container runtimes don't terminate Pods or containers for excessive CPU usage.

279: see the [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) section.

102: ### Alternatives to Secrets
103: 
104: Rather than using a Secret to protect confidential data, you can pick from alternatives.
105: 
106: Here are some of your options:
107: 
108: - If your cloud-native component needs to authenticate to another application that you
109:   know is running within the same Kubernetes cluster, you can use a
110:   [ServiceAccount](/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/#service-account-tokens)
111:   and its tokens to identify your client.
112: - There are third-party tools that you can run, either within or outside your cluster,
113:   that manage sensitive data. For example, a service that Pods access over HTTPS,
114:   that reveals a Secret if the client correctly authenticates (for example, with a ServiceAccount
115:   token).
116: - For authentication, you can implement a custom signer for X.509 certificates, and use
117:   [CertificateSigningRequests](/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/certificate-signing-requests/)
118:   to let that custom signer issue certificates to Pods that need them.
119: - You can use a [device plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/device-plugins/)
120:   to expose node-local encryption hardware to a specific Pod. For example, you can schedule
121:   trusted Pods onto nodes that provide a Trusted Platform Module, configured out-of-band.
122: 
123: You can also combine two or more of those options, including the option to use Secret objects themselves.
124: 
125: For example: implement (or deploy) an {{< glossary_tooltip text="operator" term_id="operator-pattern" >}}
126: that fetches short-lived session tokens from an external service, and then creates Secrets based
127: on those short-lived session tokens. Pods running in your cluster can make use of the session tokens,
128: and operator ensures they are valid. This separation means that you can run Pods that are unaware of
129: the exact mechanisms for issuing and refreshing those session tokens.
130: 
131: ## Types of Secret {#secret-types}
132: 
133: When creating a Secret, you can specify its type using the `type` field of
134: the [Secret](/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/config-and-storage-resources/secret-v1/)
135: resource, or certain equivalent `kubectl` command line flags (if available).
136: The Secret type is used to facilitate programmatic handling of the Secret data.
137: 
138: Kubernetes provides several built-in types for some common usage scenarios.
139: These types vary in terms of the validations performed and the constraints
140: Kubernetes imposes on them.
141: 
142: | Built-in Type                         | Usage                                   |
143: | ------------------------------------- |---------------------------------------- |
144: | `Opaque`                              | arbitrary user-defined data            |
145: | `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` | ServiceAccount token                    |
146: | `kubernetes.io/dockercfg`             | serialized `~/.dockercfg` file          |
147: | `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`      | serialized `~/.docker/config.json` file |
148: | `kubernetes.io/basic-auth`            | credentials for basic authentication    |
149: | `kubernetes.io/ssh-auth`              | credentials for SSH authentication      |
150: | `kubernetes.io/tls`                   | data for a TLS client or server         |
151: | `bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token`       | bootstrap token data                    |
152: 
153: You can define and use your own Secret type by assigning a non-empty string as the
154: `type` value for a Secret object (an empty string is treated as an `Opaque` type).

**Decision: revise before production approval.** The proposal combines useful controls, but they do not establish an end-to-end availability or data-safety guarantee. The recommendations below distinguish documented behavior from configuration choices and prerequisites.

All source paths below are local, relative to the supplied `docs/` directory; line ranges refer to source lines.

1. **PDB protection depends on the disruption.** During **node failure**, `minAvailable: 5` cannot prevent lost replicas; involuntary disruptions count against the budget afterward. During an **eviction-based node drain**, it constrains admitted evictions: with six healthy replicas, one can be evicted before further eviction must wait. Direct deletion bypasses it. During a **Deployment rolling update**, unavailable Pods count against the budget, but the Deployment is not constrained by the PDB. Consequently, `maxUnavailable: 2` permits availability to fall to four. Recommend `maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1`, with capacity for the extra Pod; `maxUnavailable: 1` also matches a five-replica rollout floor at six desired replicas. Neither protects against concurrent failures.  
   Sources: `concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md`, lines 99–145; `concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md`, lines 1183–1211.

2. **Configure explicit zone spreading.** Put a constraint in the Deployment Pod template using its application selector, `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, and `maxSkew: 1`. The key groups nodes with identical label values into domains. With `DoNotSchedule`, skew bounds the target domain’s matching-Pod count relative to the global minimum; unsatisfiable Pods remain Pending. `ScheduleAnyway` prefers reduced skew but permits imbalance. Six replicas can normally settle as two per zone, assuming suitable nodes and capacity. An unavailable zone complicates eligibility: affinity and taint policies affect which domains count. If it remains counted but cannot accept Pods, hard spreading can block replacements. If it disappears from eligible domains, remaining zones can accept replacements; specifying `minDomains: 3` instead makes the global minimum zero when fewer qualify, potentially blocking recovery. Choose that tradeoff explicitly; spreading does not restore failed replicas immediately.  
   Sources: `concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md`, lines 78–130, 167–185, 206–211, 605–619.

3. **Separate startup, service readiness, and recoverable failure.** Use a startup probe with a measured startup allowance, expressed through `failureThreshold × periodSeconds`. Until it succeeds, readiness and liveness probes are disabled; their configured delays begin afterward. Use readiness to indicate whether the API can serve requests, including required database availability where appropriate. Readiness failure removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints without restarting the container. Use liveness for application failures that restarting can resolve, such as deadlock; avoid making database unavailability alone a restart trigger. Startup or liveness failure reaching its threshold triggers container termination/restart under the restart policy. These endpoint semantics do not establish instantaneous interruption of existing connections.  
   Sources: `concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md`, lines 479–497, 524–528; `tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md`, lines 342–367, 398–422.

4. **Thirty seconds is a shutdown budget, not a completion promise.** The grace-period countdown begins **before** `preStop`; hook execution consumes that budget. The kubelet runs the hook before requesting the container’s TERM signal. The runtime normally sends SIGTERM, although an image’s configured stop signal may apply. Remaining processes receive SIGKILL after grace expires; an overrunning hook can receive a small, one-off two-second extension. Concurrently, terminating Service endpoints are marked terminating and `ready: false`, rather than immediately disappearing from EndpointSlices. The `serving` condition supports draining-aware consumers. Configure application shutdown to stop accepting work and finish open requests, then size grace from observed request and cleanup durations. The docs provide no guarantee that thirty seconds completes these long requests.  
   Sources: `reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1.md`, lines 1000–1008; `concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md`, lines 572–639.

5. **Set resource requests deliberately.** CPU requests affect scheduling capacity checks and typically relative CPU allocation during contention; they are not a maximum. Containers may use resources above their requests when available. CPU limits restrict CPU time through throttling, potentially affecting latency. Memory limits operate through reactive OOM killing, rather than equivalent CPU-style throttling; over-allocation need not cause an immediate kill. Set measured CPU requests on every relevant container: utilization-based HPA computes usage against requests. If relevant requests are missing, Pod CPU utilization is undefined and HPA takes no action for that metric. Inspect admitted configuration because a specified limit can become the request when none was supplied.  
   Sources: `concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md`, lines 27–66, 230–265; `tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md`, lines 89–102.

6. **Expect conservative HPA decisions.** The basic recommendation is the ceiling of current replicas multiplied by current-to-target metrics, but missing metrics and readiness modify it. Missing-metric Pods are assumed at 100% of target for downscaling and 0% for upscaling, damping changes. Not-yet-ready CPU Pods are set aside and, when considering scale-up, conservatively assumed at 0%. Readiness classification uses configurable defaults of thirty seconds for initial readiness delay and five minutes for CPU initialization. A recalculated ratio that reverses direction or falls within tolerance produces no scaling. Default downscale stabilization chooses the highest recommendation in the preceding five minutes. Reported utilization excludes these conservative adjustments, so it can appear inconsistent with scaling. Metrics Server or another appropriate metrics API provider is a prerequisite.  
   Source: `tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md`, lines 113–118, 129–218.

7. **Replace unrestricted connectivity with explicit allowances.** Select application and database Pods with default-deny ingress and egress policies, then allow approved callers to the API port, API-to-database traffic, and required DNS resolution. Ingress and egress isolation are independent. Policies combine additively: a broad allowance elsewhere can reopen traffic, and policy order cannot override it. A Pod-to-Pod connection needs both source egress and destination ingress permission; replies to allowed connections are implicitly allowed. Permit DNS to the cluster’s actual resolver using its required protocols and ports—the documented DNS Service exposes UDP/TCP 53. Validate selectors and any local resolver arrangement. Crucially, a CNI/network controller implementing NetworkPolicy is required; merely creating policies has no effect otherwise.  
   Sources: `concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md`, lines 45–81, 105–122; `tasks/administer-cluster/dns-debugging-resolution.md`, lines 158–174.

8. **Reject base64 credentials in Git as a protection mechanism.** Base64 obscures data; it does not make it secret. Move usable credentials out of ordinary repository manifests into a controlled delivery mechanism. Kubernetes Secrets are unencrypted in etcd by default: enable encryption at rest, restrict Secret access through least-privilege RBAC, and expose credentials only to necessary containers. Encryption of cluster storage does not protect repository copies. Restrict workload creation too: permission to create Pods, including indirectly through Deployments, can provide access to any Secret in that namespace. Secret-read restrictions alone therefore do not establish confidentiality.  
   Source: `concepts/configuration/secret.md`, lines 35–48, 305–307, 453–457.

9. **Treat PV reclamation and PVC retention as separate decisions.** Dynamically provisioned PVs inherit their StorageClass reclaim policy at creation; changing the class does not retrofit existing PVs. Inspect and edit existing PV policies individually. `Retain` leaves released storage and its data for manual reclamation after PVC deletion. Supported `Delete` behavior removes both the PV and backing storage; it is the StorageClass default. StatefulSet deletion or downscaling retains template PVCs by default, unlike explicit PVC deletion. Optional `whenDeleted` and `whenScaled` retention settings can delete affected PVCs, then the PV reclaim policy governs storage disposal. Verify the documented controller/API-server feature-gate prerequisite before depending on that behavior.  
   Sources: `concepts/storage/storage-classes.md`, lines 126–135; `concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md`, lines 178–210; `concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset.md`, lines 391–423.

10. **Validate in priority order.** First remove credential exposure and inspect existing PV reclamation settings. Second verify encryption, RBAC, CNI enforcement, permitted database access, and DNS. Third deploy measured requests, probes, shutdown handling, zone constraints, and the revised rollout; retain at least six desired replicas through HPA configuration if that is the operating baseline. Finally exercise rollout, eviction-based drain, abrupt node/zone loss, missing metrics, and disposable PVC deletion. Validate at least these unresolved limits: request completion and endpoint propagation during shutdown; surviving-zone capacity and scheduling; CPU-based scaling’s relationship to application latency; and database failover, storage accessibility, and recoverability. The documents describe control behavior, not successful outcomes for this application or cluster.
